entry.title: AI Coding Agents Increase Code Volume Without Increasing Software Output
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | arstechnica.com | source | hacker news

A study by Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton reveals that AI coding agents increase code volume by approximately 30% without leading to a proportional increase in completed software. Instead, the rapid generation of code has created a bottleneck in human-led code reviews, where the time required to merge pull requests has increased by 49%.

The research, based on data from Jellyfish, shows that pull requests requiring revisions have nearly doubled and comments per pull request have risen by 35% since the introduction of AI agents. Although 80% of measured firms use some form of AI code review, human oversight remains the primary driver of the review process, as AI agents are currently responsible for only a small fraction of total review comments and pull requests.

entry.title: Byte Language Models Demonstrate Superior Scaling and Emergent Abstractions
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | arxiv.org | source | discussion

Byte-level language models that process text as raw bytes can outperform subword-based Transformers as model size scales when utilizing token-superposition training and hash embeddings. While the longer sequences increase computational requirements, they provide a beneficial increase in total computation per parameter, allowing the models to leverage larger training data volumes effectively.

These models develop implicit, internal text abstractions that function similarly to explicit tokenizers. These learned structures allow for more efficient speculative decoding, producing a higher rate of accepted tokens than subword models. Furthermore, byte-level representations improve performance in fine-grained tasks, including optical character recognition (OCR) and word manipulation.
